title: Draft development charge study update
subtitle: Provincial Bill 23 revenue losses, growth targets, exemptions, regional comparisons and next steps toward a 2024 by-law.
overview: A special council meeting reviewed the draft 2023 Development Charge Background Study Update. Council received the report for information {{vote:m1}}. No charges were set. This was an early look, and the final study and by-law will come later.

Consultants and staff said the calculated charge for a single detached home would rise sharply from the current rate, partly because the study now looks ahead to 2051 and includes higher construction costs and new water and wastewater needs. The charge must be phased in over five years, and provincial exemptions and discounts from Bill 23 will reduce what the City can collect. Staff estimate a large shortfall over ten years, which would fall on property taxes and water and wastewater rates unless other governments cover it.

Residents can give feedback through the City's Have Your Say campaign, which launched that day. Staff will bring back a final study and hold the statutory public meeting in October, with council considering the by-law in early 2024. Council also passed the by-law confirming the meeting's proceedings {{vote:m2}}.

decisions.detail: Council received the draft study update for information, with the final study and by-law to follow later {{vote:m1}}.

debate: A delegate who sat on the peer review committee argued that growth costs not covered by development charges would be paid by current residents through taxes and water fees. The delegate called for rescinding the housing pledge and an interim control by-law to freeze growth.

Councillors asked how the shortfall would affect tax bills. Staff said the impact would come through the multi-year budget and depends on provincial rules for exemptions that are not yet released. One councillor's rough estimate suggested several years of increases of more than 8% if it were all funded from property taxes. Staff said the cost is spread across taxes and water, wastewater and stormwater rates.

Some councillors questioned whether the study should use the 18,000-unit housing pledge rather than about 12,700 units. Staff said updating master plans and budgets would take years, and the study can be updated sooner if growth outpaces the forecast. A councillor asked staff to consider building in a trigger for that update.

Several councillors asked that the October version show the shortfall clearly in its tables. Staff agreed to add a table. Others asked about charging by home size or bedrooms and about incentives for smaller units. Staff said this is possible but tied to how servicing needs are measured, and they will look at it.

A councillor asked for outlooks on when neighbouring municipalities will update their charges, to judge competitiveness for industry. Staff agreed to provide this and said feedback on discretionary exemptions is welcome over the summer.
